tagline.text: Iloilo's oldest surviving mansion, built in 1803 in Jaro

location.label: Location
location.text: Santa Isabel Street, Jaro district, Iloilo City (near Jaro Cathedral)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100~500 (per person, covering transport, snacks and a maintenance donation)

children.text: Casa Mariquit is a house built in 1803 on Santa Isabel Street in the Jaro district of Iloilo City, and it is described as the oldest surviving mansion in Iloilo. It is a small house museum where you can see furniture and photographs of the Javellana-Lopez family.
Casa Mariquit is a heritage house on Santa Isabel Street in Jaro, the old aristocratic district of Iloilo City. Wikipedia lists it as completed in

and describes it as the oldest surviving mansion in Iloilo. It is also known as the Javellana-Lopez Heritage House. The coordinates given by Wikipedia (about 10.727 N, 122.557 E) lie close to Jaro Cathedral in the same district (about 10.724 N, 122.556 E), so it is easy to visit while walking around the cathedral area. It is described as lying about
3~4km
northwest of the city center.

The history of the house is tied to a family that built its wealth on banking and sugar. According to Wikipedia, a Javellana banker built the house as both a bank and a residence, and it later became the home of his granddaughter Maria Salvacion "Mariquit" Javellana and her husband Fernando Lopez Sr. Fernando Lopez served as Vice President of the Philippines in 1949~1953 and 1965~1972. The name comes from his wife's nickname, "Mariquit," which a 2016 BusinessMirror article suggests may derive from the Tagalog word "marikit" (beautiful). Sources disagree on the builder's name (Ramon Javellana, Julio Quiambong Javellana and others), so this guide simply says "a banker of the Javellana family."

The building is classified as a bahay na bato, the traditional Philippine house of stone and wood. The ground floor once housed a bank, while the upper floor was the living space where the family lived and received guests. According to the 2016 article, a cement vault believed to date from around 1900 is hidden under the wooden floorboards and can be glimpsed from the master bedroom. After the former vice president died in 1993, his great-grandson Robert Lopez Puckett Jr. began restoring the house, and it is said to remain in the care of the Javellana-Lopez family today. Wikipedia describes it as a museum open to the public for tours.

From a traveler's point of view, this is less a polished exhibition hall than a "home museum" where a wealthy family's old life has been preserved. Old cameras, wall clocks, a gramophone, paintings, keys, a chessboard, a grand grandfather clock and family photographs stand out. The large banyan tree whose roots creep toward the wall in front of the house has also become a symbol of the place. However, sources disagree on opening hours, fees and whether the door is open, so you need to check locally before you go. Knowing this, you will remember it as a small house with many stories.

Wikipedia and many travel reviews describe this house, built in 1803, as the oldest surviving heritage house in Iloilo. The biggest appeal is being able to step on wooden stairs and floors more than 200 years old. Treat "oldest" as a descriptive claim and use it for reference only.

blocks.title: The bank vault under the wooden floor

children.text: The 2016 article reports that the ground floor was once a bank and that a cement vault is hidden under the floorboards. It says the vault can be glimpsed from the master bedroom, so ask your guide to show you. It lets you imagine the wealth and security arrangements of a banking family.

blocks.title: A sealed teller window and a bench for chickens

children.text: A 2025 travel blog reports that an opening like a bank teller window remains sealed in a wall, and that an old wooden bench near the staircase has small sliding-door compartments. The guide reportedly explained that tenants left live chickens, brought as gifts, in these compartments. This comes from a single source, so ask on site.

Items such as a gramophone, old cameras, a grandfather clock and a chessboard are on display. The 2016 article says there are photographs of the Lopez family with foreign leaders and a photo of Pope John Paul II's visit. The Wikipedia sentence that the pope blessed the house in February 1981 is flagged as needing a better source, so do not take it as established fact.

blocks.title: The great banyan tree at the front

children.text: The large banyan tree beside the house works as a landmark for finding it and is known for roots that climb the wall. Locally it is also said to be home to spirits. Photos come out well when the afternoon light is low.

The 2016 article says the owner, Mr. Puckett, runs a solar company and put solar panels on the roof, which he called a "small concession to modernization." A 200-year-old house alongside modern electrical equipment is an interesting sight.

According to reviews, the person who looks after the house tells its stories in person. One blog says a caretaker called Bon Bon grew up on the property and has made restoring it his life's work. Hearing the family story and hidden details firsthand is far more vivid than reading signboards.

blocks.title: A starting point for a Jaro heritage walk

children.text: The house is close to Jaro Cathedral, and other heritage houses such as the Lopez Heritage House and the Lizares Mansion are said to be in the same district. It suits a half-day route linking old houses and the cathedral on foot.
Travel from central Iloilo to the Jaro district by jeepney, taxi or tricycle. It is about
3~4km
from downtown, described as taking roughly
10~15 minutes
Get off at Jaro Cathedral square, look around the cathedral first, then walk toward Santa Isabel Street. The house is described as within walking distance of the cathedral.
Arrive at Casa Mariquit and photograph the banyan tree and the front of the house. If the main door is closed, try the side gate or the back to find the caretaker.
Follow the caretaker through the former bank area on the ground floor, the wooden staircase, and the upstairs living room, master bedroom and belongings. Ask permission before taking photos.
When the tour ends, give an entrance donation or a tip in cash. Sources differ on the fee, but many reviews say around
, so follow the local guidance.
Move on to another heritage house in Jaro or a restaurant near the cathedral square.
Opening hours and visiting arrangements differ between sources. If your schedule is fixed, check locally before you set out.

items.title: Half-day Jaro heritage walk
items.subtitle: Cathedral and heritage house in one day

children.text: Have breakfast in central Iloilo and head to the Jaro district.
Visit Jaro Cathedral. Taking the cathedral and plaza slowly takes about
40 minutes
Tour Casa Mariquit. Look for the banyan tree, the staircase, the vault traces and the family belongings.
Check whether other heritage houses in the district (such as the Lopez Heritage House) are open, and stop by if time allows.
Have lunch of local Iloilo food, then return to the city center.
Flights run from Manila (NAIA) to Iloilo International Airport (ILO), with a flight time of about
1 hour 10 to 25 minutes
(varies slightly by flight; check locally by airline and season).
The airport is some distance from the city, so take a taxi or airport van into the city and then on to Jaro. Check fares and travel times locally.

items.title: By boat and bus from Manila

children.text: If you have plenty of time, you can combine boats and buses from Manila, but schedules change often. Check the latest schedule with the shipping line.

items.title: From the city center to Jaro

children.text: By car it is described as about
3~4km
from downtown and
10~15 minutes
. Street parking in front of the house is limited.
By public transport, take a jeepney or tricycle toward Jaro and get off near Santa Isabel Street. You can also walk from Jaro Cathedral.
When calling a Grab or taxi, it helps to show the address (20 Santa Isabel St, Jaro).
The house visit is mostly indoors, so weather matters little, but walking around Jaro is easier when it is not rainy. The November–May dry season is recommended.

In March–May, when midday heat is intense, go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, and bring an umbrella in the rainy season. To avoid a wasted trip to a closed door, early morning is recommended.

Jaro is close to central Iloilo, so most travelers stay at hotels in the city and come for a day trip. Hotels in the city center or near the Esplanade make getting around easy. Hotel names and rates change often, so check the latest information on a booking site.

You can eat around Jaro Cathedral square or in the city's restaurant districts. Iloilo is a city known for its local food, so after the house visit it is a good idea to head into the city and add a local meal. Check that a restaurant is open before choosing it.
Check locally whether visits are possible before you leave. A 2016 article recommended calling for an appointment, and a 2025 blog says the front door was locked.
If the front door is closed, look for the caretaker at the back or by the side gate.
Fees are sometimes taken as a donation rather than an entrance fee or guide charge, so carry small bills in cash.
Ask permission before taking photos, and inquire in advance about professional shoots.
Combine your visit with Jaro Cathedral on the same day.
The old wooden floors and stairs call for non-slip shoes and slow steps.
Ask the caretaker about the house's history and hidden spaces, and the commentary becomes much richer.
Opening hours and fees differ between sources and the house may be closed, so check locally before you visit.
Fee information conflicts between ₱50 and free. Confirm the latest arrangement locally.
It is a privately owned house, so the door may be closed or tours limited depending on circumstances.
The old house has narrow, dim areas, and some visitors have described it as eerie in reviews.
Unlike typical tourist sites, there may be few route signs, so follow the caretaker's guidance and requests.
The leading church of the Jaro district, within walking distance. It makes a good pairing.
About
3~4km
from the city center, which is the base for lodging, restaurants and transport.
A riverside promenade reached from the city center, well suited to an evening stroll.
A well-known church in the Molo district of the same city, good to combine with Jaro in a day route.
